name: Battens at sixteen inches on centre
symptom: Vertical siding in which the battens are spaced at a machine interval — 12, 16 or 24 in on centre — over a sheet product, so the batten covers a stud rather than a board joint. Battens are 2 1/2 in wide and 1/2 to 5/8 in thick, in a shallow relief that dies at any distance. A 48 in panel joint is usually visible as a slightly different shadow at every fourth batten. Frequently the siding stops at a storey line and clapboard begins.

cause.explanation: Vertical boarding has been replaced by 4x8 or 4x9 engineered panels with a grooved face. The battens then have nothing to cover, so they are set at a fastening interval instead. The panel's own edges must land on studs at 48 in, which is not a multiple of 16 that reads as anything, so the field battens are at 16 in and the joint battens are at 48. The result is a wall with two different battens doing two different jobs and no way to tell which is which.
cause.cost_saved: Panel-and-batten runs $5-$9/sf; true board-and-batten in solid stock runs $11-$20/sf. Across 1,800 sf of wall, $10,000-$20,000.

rule_violated.ref: a batten covers a joint between boards
rule_violated.statement: Batten spacing is therefore a consequence of board width, and board widths in real work are irregular. A perfectly regular batten spacing is a declaration that there are no boards underneath.
True Downing practice runs battens unbroken from water table to eave; if the vertical siding stops and clapboard begins at a storey line, the house is later and cheaper.
Carpenter Gothic. Vertical boarding has no colonial Georgian existence.

correct_practice: Boards first, battens second. Boards run 8-12 in wide with a mixture of widths, laid vertically with a 1/4 to 3/8 in gap at each joint for movement; battens are 2 1/2 to 3 1/2 in wide and not less than 3/4 in thick, centred on each joint, so the spacing follows the boards and varies from 8 1/2 to 12 1/2 in on centre. Every batten runs unbroken from the water table to the eave — that continuity is what makes the wall vertical, and it is the specific thing Downing's practice insisted on. The batten must be thicker than the pattern needs: a 3/4 in batten on a 1 in board throws a 3/4 in shadow on each side, which is what produces the strongly striped surface the style is after, and a 1/2 in batten on a grooved panel throws about 1/4 in and produces nothing. Where the wall meets a horizontal, the battens die into a real member with a wash — a water table below and a frieze above — not into a caulk joint.

fixes.right: Solid boards of varied width with battens on the joints, 3/4 to 1 1/8 in thick, running full height from the water table to the frieze.
fixes.cheap: Keep the panel and fix the batten. Two changes, neither expensive: make the battens 1 1/8 in thick instead of 5/8 (about $0.60/lf, or $400 a house) and vary the spacing across the wall by grouping them in an irregular but repeating rhythm — 10, 12, 9, 11 in rather than 16, 16, 16, 16. Thickness buys the shadow and irregularity buys the reading of boards. Then hide the panel joints by putting a WIDER batten (4 in) at 48 in centres and treating it as an intentional secondary rhythm rather than an accident.
fixes.dishonest: A pre-grooved panel with a printed or embossed 'batten' moulded into the sheet at 8 in centres. It has the spacing right and the depth zero, so it reads correct in a catalogue photograph at 3 ft and as a flat wall at 30. It also cannot be re-detailed later, because there is nothing to add a batten to.

detection: Measure the spacing and look for a repeating machine number. Battens at a constant 12, 16 or 24 in are a machine interval; battens at varying 8-13 in are boards. Then look for the 48 in panel joint — often a slightly wider caulk line or a subtle tone difference — which confirms sheet goods. Measure the batten's shadow against its width: a correct batten's shadow is roughly its thickness, so a 3 in batten should show a 3/4-1 in dark edge on the shaded side; a hairline means a thin batten. Finally, follow one batten top to bottom: if it stops at a storey line, or if the vertical siding gives way to horizontal siding at a floor line, the fault includes a material change with no plane change as well.

exceptions.why: Board-and-batten is not merely permitted here, it is the correct and characteristic cladding, deliberately vertical to reinforce the steep gables. Downing argued for it explicitly.
exceptions.bounds: Requires the rest of the type: 12:12 or steeper gables, a pierced bargeboard, and battens running unbroken from water table to eave. Board-and-batten on a low-pitched roof is an orphan.

bounds_test.note: Requires the rest of the type — 12:12 or steeper gables and a pierced bargeboard — and the unbroken run. Board-and-batten on a low-pitched roof is an orphan.

exceptions.why: Same reasoning; vertical boarding is part of the American Gothic villa's argument.

bounds_test.note: Vertical boarding is part of the American Gothic villa's argument and depends on the steep gable it reinforces.

exceptions.why: Board-and-batten is authentic on outbuildings, barns, sheds and the service ends of farmhouses, where it was the cheapest weathertight wall available and the irregular board widths are genuine.
exceptions.bounds: Legitimate on subordinate volumes and utility buildings. Its appearance on the principal front of a house that is otherwise Colonial Revival is an anachronism — board-and-batten has no Colonial existence and its use on Colonial Revival work is a 2010s fashion, not a revival of anything.

bounds_test.note: Authentic on outbuildings, barns, sheds and the service ends of farmhouses, where irregular board widths are genuine. Its appearance on the principal front of an otherwise Colonial Revival house is an anachronism, not a vernacular survival.

exceptions.why: The idiom has adopted board-and-batten knowingly as a contemporary gesture rather than as a historical claim.
exceptions.bounds: Honest only where the rest of the building is equally frank. It does not excuse a 5/8 in batten: the depth rule is not stylistic, it is about whether the wall casts shadows.

bounds_test.note: Honest only where the rest of the building is equally frank, and the depth rule is not stylistic — it is about whether the wall casts shadows. The primary test is unchanged.

confused_with.difference: Board-and-batten stopping at a storey line and turning into clapboard is that fault as well as this one. Diagnose both.
Both are applied vertical members that should describe something underneath. The batten describes a joint; the timber describes a frame. The tests are different but the disease is the same.

sources: A. J. Downing, The Architecture of Country Houses (1850), on vertical boarding and battens
LP SmartSide and James Hardie panel installation instructions (48 in panel module, batten fastening)

test.note: A 3/4 in batten on a 1 in board throws a 3/4 in shadow on each side, which is what produces the strongly striped vertical surface the style is after. A 1/2 in batten on a grooved panel throws about 1/4 in and produces nothing. Measure the shadow against the batten's own width — a correct batten's shadow is roughly its thickness, so a 3 in batten shows a 3/4-1 in dark edge on the shaded side.

secondary_tests.note: A batten covers a joint between boards, and board widths in real work are irregular — 8-12 in giving spacings of 8 1/2 to 12 1/2 in on centre. A constant 12, 16 or 24 in is a machine interval and a declaration that there are no boards underneath. Near-zero variation is the fault's signature.
Battens run 2 1/2 to 3 1/2 in wide. Narrower and the stripe is thin; wider and the wall becomes panelled.

Downing's specific insistence and the style node's own tell: true practice runs battens unbroken from water table to eave. A batten stopping at a storey line, or vertical siding giving way to horizontal siding at a floor line, fails here and commits material-change-with-no-plane-change as well.

severity_by_style.why: Vertical boarding is the cladding the style is built on, and the node's own tell is that ornament projects less than about two inches because everything came off a plank — the battens are the one place depth was expected.
The idiom has adopted board-and-batten knowingly as a contemporary gesture, so the anachronism charge does not stick; the depth rule still does.
Board-and-batten has no colonial existence at all, so its appearance on a Colonial Revival front is an anachronism before it is a depth fault.
